A cowlick is a small patch of hair on a person's scalp that grows in a noticeably different direction from all the hair around it. Instead of lying flat and blending in smoothly, this section sticks up, swirls outward, or points in a direction of its own. The result is a tuft or spiral that looks out of place compared to the rest of the hair — almost as if someone pressed a finger against the hair and twirled it, except no one did.

Cowlicks most commonly appear at the crown of the head — that's the upper-back area of the scalp. However, they can also show up at the front hairline (often right above the forehead, creating a little wave or spike), at the nape of the neck, or anywhere else on the scalp. Some people have just one; others have two or more.

Every hair on your head grows out of a tiny opening in the skin called a follicle, and each follicle sits at a slight angle — this angle determines which way the hair leans as it grows. Normally, the follicles in a given area all point in roughly the same direction, so the hair lies neatly together. In the area of a cowlick, though, a cluster of follicles points in a conflicting direction. Because the hairs in that spot are literally growing the "wrong" way relative to their neighbors, they stick out. This is not something that happens to you — you are born with it, and it is determined by your genetics.

A cowlick has a stubborn, spring-like quality. You can comb it flat, but it will bounce back up as soon as the comb leaves. Wet hair temporarily tames a cowlick because water weighs the hair down and makes it more pliable, but as the hair dries, the cowlick reasserts itself. Cowlicks tend to be more visible and more bothersome when hair is cut short, because longer hair is heavier and its weight helps hold the rebel section down.

No, not without professional chemical treatments. The follicles responsible for a cowlick will always grow hair in that direction — you cannot retrain them through combing or brushing alone. However, people manage cowlicks in several practical ways: growing hair longer so the weight suppresses it, using styling gel or pomade to hold it in place, blow-drying it against its natural direction while it's still damp (which can flatten it temporarily), or working with a hairstylist to design a cut that uses the cowlick's direction as a deliberate stylistic feature rather than fighting it. Many hairstylists actually consider cowlick placement when deciding how to cut someone's hair.

They are extremely common — a large portion of people have at least one. They are not a flaw or a medical issue in any way; they are simply a natural variation in hair growth. Children often have very prominent cowlicks, particularly at the crown or hairline, and these are considered entirely normal.

"Cowlick" is used specifically and almost exclusively to describe this hair phenomenon. You would say things like: "I can never style my hair the way I want because of this cowlick at the back of my head," or "The little boy had a cowlick that made the front of his hair stick straight up." It is a neutral, everyday word — not rude, not technical, not informal slang. Anyone from a child to a doctor to a hairstylist would use it without hesitation.
